title: Tier 2 escalation webhook and platform event

requirement.summary: Build a Tier 2 Case-escalation notification path: when a Case moves into the existing Tier_2_Engineering queue, an Apex Queueable (enqueued off the escalation-triggering automation, authenticated via a Named Credential + External Credential holding the on-call tool's API key) posts case number, severity, subject and a case link to an HTTPS on-call-tool webhook with status-code-based retry, and the same escalation publishes a Platform Event that an already-subscribed internal ops dashboard consumes; every delivery attempt lands on a new, admin-visible failure/audit record with a manual resend action, and the API key is held only in an External Credential, never in code or a Custom Setting.

clarifications.question: Per standards/decision-trees/integration-pattern-selection.md Direction 1 (Salesforce calls out): confirm the on-call webhook call is fire-and-forget (Queueable, not Continuation, since no user watches a spinner), authenticated via Named Credential + External Credential (Custom header / API key per Q2), and retried per a status-code classification (Q4) — does the on-call tool's actual contract match this shape, or does it require something else (e.g. a synchronous ack, OAuth instead of a static key)?
clarifications.why: This is the tree's own top-level direction/auth/retry checklist; a wrong call here is a rebuild of the whole integration shape, not a tweak.
clarifications.proposed_default: Fire-and-forget Queueable, Named Credential + External Credential with Custom header (API key), retry classified by status code.
clarifications.answer_shape: A direction/auth/retry row naming the pattern actually used, or the deviation and why.
clarifications.answer: Confirmed: Direction 1 only — Salesforce calls out to the on-call tool's HTTPS REST endpoint (JSON POST). Nothing calls into Salesforce for this feature.

clarifications.question: Reject the legacy Outbound Message / Workflow Rule action mechanism in favor of a Named-Credential-based Apex callout for the on-call notification — confirm?
clarifications.why: Outbound Message's host (Workflow Rules) reached end of support 31 Dec 2025, cannot express JSON + API-key auth cleanly (it expects a SOAP Ack envelope), and this decision determines every downstream metadata choice.
clarifications.proposed_default: Yes — use a Named-Credential-based Apex callout, not Outbound Message.
clarifications.answer_shape: A yes/no plus the rejected-alternative reason recorded in decisions.md.
clarifications.answer: Yes. Reject Outbound Message / Workflow Rule. Use a Named Credential + Apex callout so the key lives in an External Credential and retries/failure records are under our control.

clarifications.question: Is the on-call tool's Named Credential built on the Legacy model or the enhanced SecuredEndpoint model (separate External Credential)?
clarifications.why: Every field the Legacy shape relies on is deprecated at API 56.0; building new metadata on it means building on a deprecated surface.
clarifications.proposed_default: SecuredEndpoint (Named Credential + separate External Credential).
clarifications.answer_shape: The namedCredentialType value and the file count it implies (2 vs 1).
clarifications.answer: Enhanced model: a Named Credential on top of a separate External Credential (SecuredEndpoint). No legacy Named Credential.

clarifications.question: Named principal or per-user principal for the on-call tool's External Credential?
clarifications.why: Only Named Principal works from Batch, Queueable and Scheduled Apex — this design requires a Queueable, so the principal type is not a free choice.
clarifications.proposed_default: Named Principal — required for the Queueable-based callout.
clarifications.answer_shape: NamedPrincipal vs PerUserPrincipal, with the Queueable constraint cited as the reason.
clarifications.answer: Named principal — one service API key for the whole org. Per-user principals are not wanted; the on-call tool has one integration user.

clarifications.question: Who owns the Authorization header on the webhook call — does the External Credential inject it (generateAuthorizationHeader default true), or does the Apex code build it explicitly?
clarifications.why: Apex adding its own header on top of the platform default is a documented collision that surfaces as a 401.
clarifications.proposed_default: The platform / External Credential owns it; Apex does not set an Authorization header itself.
clarifications.answer_shape: One named owner for the header, encoded in the External Credential metadata.
clarifications.answer: The External Credential injects the API key as a custom header; Apex never reads or builds the Authorization/API-key header and never sees the secret.

clarifications.question: Does the on-call tool expect the API key in a specific custom header name, or in the request body?
clarifications.why: This decides the External Credential parameter shape ({!$Credential.*} merge field target) and whether allowMergeFieldsInHeader / allowMergeFieldsInBody must be enabled — both default false.
clarifications.answer_shape: The exact header name (or body path) the vendor's API documents.
clarifications.answer: A custom header named X-API-Key (the tool's documented header). The request body is JSON.

clarifications.question: For the on-call tool's API specifically, which HTTP status codes are transient/retryable (e.g. 429, 503) and which indicate a hard failure that should go straight to the visible failure record (e.g. 401, 422)?
clarifications.why: Retryable vs non-retryable cannot be inferred from the status code alone; retrying a 401 is a lockout, not a fix.
clarifications.answer_shape: A status-code classification table the retry logic and its tests both read.
clarifications.answer: Transient/retryable: 429, 502, 503, 504 and connection timeouts (retry up to 3 times with backoff). Permanent: 400, 401, 403, 404, 422 — no retry, write the failure record immediately.

clarifications.question: Is the webhook POST safe to send twice, and does the on-call tool accept/require an idempotency key?
clarifications.why: A 5xx or transport failure means unknown, not failed; retrying without a key can double-page the same escalation.
clarifications.answer_shape: Either a documented idempotency-key header, or an explicit no-retry-on-ambiguous-outcome decision.
clarifications.answer: Yes, the POST is safe to send twice; the tool accepts an Idempotency-Key header. Use the Case Id plus the escalation timestamp as the key.

clarifications.question: Per standards/decision-trees/async-selection.md Q2-Q4: confirm the escalation-triggered work is fire-and-forget (not user-facing), runs from a Queueable (AllowsCallouts) enqueued off the Case-escalation automation, and decide the publish sequencing — does the platform event publish before the callout (dashboard sees the escalation immediately regardless of webhook outcome) or after it (event carries the callout's outcome too)?
clarifications.why: This is the tree's own entry-point classification plus the one sequencing decision the tree does not make for you; it changes what the Queueable's execute() actually does and in what order.
clarifications.proposed_default: Publish the platform event first (dashboard visibility should not depend on webhook success), then attempt the callout with retry.
clarifications.answer_shape: The chosen sequencing, with the rejected order's reason recorded.
clarifications.answer: Fire-and-forget: no user waits on the result. It must complete within a minute of the escalation, which a Queueable enqueued from the after-update handler satisfies.

clarifications.question: If the Case-escalation transaction that triggers this automation rolls back, must the on-call tool and the ops dashboard still be notified?
clarifications.why: Decides the Platform Event object's publishBehavior element; omitting it defaults to PublishImmediately, which fires regardless of rollback.
clarifications.proposed_default: No — publish only after the Case save commits (PublishAfterCommit); a rolled-back escalation should not page anyone.
clarifications.answer_shape: The explicit publishBehavior value and which limit meter the publisher spends.
clarifications.answer: If the escalation transaction rolls back, nothing must reach the on-call tool or the dashboard. Enqueue the callout and publish the event only when the transaction commits (publish-after-commit semantics).

clarifications.question: What is the worst-case impact if one escalation's platform event is silently lost (EventBus.publish success only means 'queued', not 'delivered')?
clarifications.why: Decides whether checking Database.SaveResult is enough or an EventPublishFailureCallback plus a logged-failure path is required.
clarifications.answer_shape: Either an accepted-risk note, or the failure callback wired into the same failure record as the webhook path.
clarifications.answer: Worst case a Severity 1 escalation is missing from the ops dashboard. The webhook is the primary channel; a lost event is tolerable when the webhook succeeded, but the publish result must be checked and a failed publish logged in the same failure record object.

clarifications.question: What happens if the ops dashboard processes the same escalation event twice (Platform Events deliver at-least-once)?
clarifications.why: Decides whether the event payload needs a stable EventUuid / case number the dashboard can dedupe on, which is a contract with a team this build does not own.
clarifications.proposed_default: Dashboard dedupes on case number / EventUuid; document as a contract with the dashboard's owning team, not solved on the Salesforce side.
clarifications.answer_shape: The dedupe key named in the event schema, and confirmation the dashboard team has agreed to use it.
clarifications.answer: The dashboard team will dedupe on case number + escalation time; duplicate events are acceptable. Do not add Salesforce-side dedupe for the event.

clarifications.question: Where is the callout Queueable enqueued from (the escalation-triggering automation directly, or a service layer), and could that same code path ever run from inside another async job?
clarifications.why: The enqueue ceiling differs by context — 50 per synchronous transaction, exactly 1 per asynchronous transaction — and a callout cannot follow DML in the same execute().
clarifications.answer_shape: The one call site that owns the enqueue, and confirmation it is never itself inside another async transaction.
clarifications.answer: Enqueued from the Case after-update trigger handler's service layer: one Queueable per transaction carrying every escalated Case Id in that transaction (bulk-safe), not one per case.

clarifications.question: Can the same escalation be enqueued twice from two different transactions (e.g. a re-save, a duplicate escalation trigger firing)? If so, is cross-transaction dedup needed?
clarifications.why: A static in-memory guard resets at the transaction boundary; only AsyncOptions.DuplicateSignature suppresses duplicates across transactions, and a suppressed enqueue throws rather than silently no-op'ing.
clarifications.answer_shape: The stable business key (likely Case Id) the DuplicateSignature is built from, and the catch that turns the exception into a no-op.
clarifications.answer: Yes, a re-save can re-fire. Stamp a new field Case.Tier2_Notified_At__c when the webhook succeeds and skip cases already stamped within the last 10 minutes.

clarifications.question: When the Queueable throws an unhandled or limit exception, must the failure record still get written?
clarifications.why: try/catch cannot survive a limit exception that terminates the transaction; only a Finalizer runs either way, and its budget is five consecutive re-enqueues.
clarifications.proposed_default: Yes — a Finalizer writes/updates the failure record on both SUCCESS and UNHANDLED_EXCEPTION, since that is the only guaranteed hook.
clarifications.answer_shape: The Finalizer's behavior on each terminal state, named explicitly.
clarifications.answer: Yes. The failure record must be written even when the Queueable dies on an unhandled or limit exception — use a Queueable Finalizer for that.

clarifications.question: Where does the visible failure record live — a new custom object dedicated to this integration, or does Apex already have a sink (e.g. templates/apex/custom_objects/Application_Log__c) that should be reused/extended instead of inventing a new one?
clarifications.why: One sink is queryable, correlatable and reportable; two sinks are two half-monitored portfolios that need a join nobody has written.
clarifications.answer_shape: One named object (new or reused), and a reason if a new one is chosen over the existing log sink.
clarifications.answer: A new custom object dedicated to this integration: Integration_Failure__c. We have no existing Apex log object in the org.

clarifications.question: What does the status/severity picklist on the failure record contain, and does the Apex code send exactly those values?
clarifications.why: A required + restricted picklist that the sending code doesn't match exactly makes the fault-path write itself fault, and then nothing is logged at all.
clarifications.proposed_default: A restricted picklist (e.g. Pending / Failed / Retrying / Resolved) with values matching the Apex enum exactly.
clarifications.answer_shape: The exact picklist value list, cross-checked against the Apex constant list.
clarifications.answer: Status picklist: New, Retrying, Resent, Resolved, Abandoned. Severity picklist: Error, Warning. Apex must write exactly those values and nothing else.

clarifications.question: What fields must the failure record carry to make a resend actionable?
clarifications.why: A permanent failure that only leaves a debug-log line is invisible; the record needs enough to both diagnose and replay the call.
clarifications.proposed_default: Case lookup, Request_Payload__c (long text), Last_Error__c, Retry_Count__c, Status__c, Last_Attempted_Date__c.
clarifications.answer_shape: The field list, each with the value it must hold to support a one-click resend.
clarifications.answer: Case lookup, case number, endpoint, HTTP status, response body (first 32k chars), attempt count, last attempt time, error message, the JSON payload sent, Status, and a Resend checkbox the admin ticks.

clarifications.question: Which permission set grants External Credential principal access and the failure-record's CRUD/FLS, and who/what is it assigned to (the Automated Process running user, a named integration user, the admins who need to see and resend failures)?
clarifications.why: A principal is inert until externalCredentialPrincipalAccesses grants it, and nothing in the deploy fails without it — the integration returns 401 for every user until this is explicit; record access and field access are separate mechanisms configured in different places.
clarifications.answer_shape: A sharing_impact value naming the layer plus a named permission set and its assignees.
clarifications.answer: A permission set Tier2_Webhook_Admin grants Integration_Failure__c CRUD/FLS and the External Credential principal access; assigned to the three Support Engineering admins. The Automated Process user's access to the principal is granted the way the named-credentials skill prescribes; call out in the plan if that needs a separate step.

clarifications.question: Who is allowed to resend a failed webhook, and is that the same team that reviews the failure backlog?
clarifications.why: Resend is a write action with real side effects (re-paging the on-call tool); an unnamed owner for that action is a rumour, not a control.
clarifications.answer_shape: A named role or permission set assignee, and confirmation they are the same audience that triages the backlog.
clarifications.answer: Support Engineering resends (by ticking Resend on the failure record); the same team reviews the backlog.

clarifications.question: Once a webhook delivery fails and lands in the visible failure record, what is the response-time expectation for someone to notice and resend it, and who is on the hook?
clarifications.why: "Make it visible" hides the trigger, the exception path and the owner of the failure; without a named owner and a target, the record is a rumour with a UI.
clarifications.answer_shape: The exception path and a named owner, which is what makes the resend flow estimable.
clarifications.answer: A failed delivery must be looked at within 4 business hours; the backlog is reviewed daily.

clarifications.question: What is the real steady-state volume of Tier 2 escalations (per hour and per day) and the worst-case single burst, so retry/backoff sizing, Queueable chunking and the Platform Event publishing-allocation budget (250,000/hour EE/PE/UE) are sized correctly?
clarifications.why: Automation that passes UAT on ten records fails on a real burst; the publishing allocation is an hourly ceiling shared with every other publisher in the org.
clarifications.answer_shape: A data_volume value with a steady-state number and a worst-case batch number.
clarifications.answer: Steady state about 15 Tier 2 escalations a day, peaking at 2 an hour; worst single burst 50 escalations in 5 minutes during a major incident.

clarifications.question: Should the Queueable class run in system mode or explicit user/sharing mode, given it fires as the Automated Process entity rather than an interactive user?
clarifications.why: Outside system mode the running user needs View Setup and Configuration to enqueue asynchronous Apex at all, and from API 67.0 an undeclared class runs with sharing by default where it used to run without — the wrong choice either over-exposes data or silently fails to enqueue.
clarifications.proposed_default: Without sharing / system mode, typical for an escalation-triggered background job with no per-user data exposure concern — confirm no FLS/CRUD bypass risk before accepting.
clarifications.answer_shape: The explicit sharing declaration and the permission set that carries the enqueue right.
clarifications.answer: Run the Queueable with sharing in the API 67 default user mode; it executes as the Automated Process entity, so the plan must state how that entity gets create access on Integration_Failure__c and the principal access — treat as a design point to settle in the plan, not something to guess.

clarifications.question: Who is alerted, and how, when the whole notification channel silently stops working (not a single failed delivery, but the subscription/automation itself going dark)?
clarifications.why: Nothing in Apex reports a dead event subscription or a disabled trigger on its own; a per-delivery failure record does not catch the channel itself failing.
clarifications.answer_shape: A scheduled health-check query and a named recipient, so a month-long gap becomes a same-day one.
clarifications.answer: A scheduled hourly check (flow or Apex — planner's choice by the async tree) that emails Support Engineering when more than 3 failures land in an hour or no success has occurred in 24 hours while escalations exist. Sender is the org-wide address support-noreply@acme.example, which is a deploy prerequisite (it must be verified in the target org first).

clarifications.proposed_default: e.g. OnCall_Tool, identical across all environments, with the endpoint URL parameterized per org.

decisions.decision: Salesforce calls out to the on-call tool fire-and-forget from a Queueable implementing Database.AllowsCallouts; nothing calls into Salesforce for this feature.
decisions.branch_quote: ├── No, fire-and-forget                     → Queueable with AllowsCallouts
decisions.rationale: Q1's answer confirms Direction 1 only and Q9 confirms no user waits on the result, which is exactly this branch. Continuation is excluded because nobody watches a spinner; Batch is excluded because the volume is 15 a day peaking at 50 in five minutes (Q22).
alternatives_rejected: Outbound Message on a Workflow Rule
decisions.consequences: The notification is decoupled from the save, so a webhook outage never blocks a Support agent's escalation - and the only evidence a notification failed is the Integration_Failure__c row this build creates.

decisions.decision: Authenticate with a Named Credential over a separate External Credential using the Custom authentication protocol, with the API key injected as the X-API-Key header by the credential rather than by Apex.
decisions.branch_quote: ├── Custom header / API key                 → Named Credential + External Credential (Custom)
decisions.rationale: Q6 names X-API-Key as the tool's documented header and Q5 assigns header ownership to the platform, so generateAuthorizationHeader is deployed false and the header is an ExternalCredential AuthHeader parameter. Apex sets no credential header at all, so allowMergeFieldsInHeader stays false.
alternatives_rejected: API key in a Custom Setting or Custom Label
Apex-built Authorization header with an Apex-side {!$Credential.*} merge field
decisions.consequences: The secret is entered in Setup against the principal after deploy and is never in source, an export, or a sandbox refresh - which also means the deploy alone does not make the integration work: a human must enter the value and assign the permission set.

decisions.decision: The External Credential declares a NamedPrincipal, not a PerUserPrincipal, and the Named Credential is the enhanced SecuredEndpoint type rather than Legacy.
decisions.rationale: integration-pattern-selection.md Q2 routes to 'Named Credential + External Credential (Custom)' but does not choose between principal types or between the legacy and enhanced models; the skill's Decision Guidance does, on both counts - 'Async job (Batch / Queueable / Scheduled) -> NamedPrincipal' and 'every legacy field is deprecated at 56.0 - new work goes on SecuredEndpoint'. Q3 and Q4 answer the same way.
alternatives_rejected: Legacy Named Credential with an embedded endpoint and protocol
decisions.consequences: One shared service identity means the on-call tool's audit trail attributes every incident to Salesforce rather than to the escalating agent; the trade is that a per-user principal would not work from a Queueable at all.

decisions.decision: The webhook body is JSON, serialised and deserialised in Apex through templates/apex/HttpClient.cls rather than a hand-built HttpRequest.
decisions.branch_quote: ├── JSON REST                               → HttpClient + JSON.serialize/deserialize
decisions.rationale: Q1 and Q6 both describe a JSON POST. Q31 sizes the payload well under the 6MB/12MB ceilings, so no paging or chunking is needed.
alternatives_rejected: Raw HttpRequest construction in the Queueable
decisions.consequences: The endpoint, the timeout and the retry switch are all set through one builder the checker recognises, which is also why the per-Case callout loop does not trip check_callouts_and_http_integrations.py rule 4.

decisions.decision: Transient failures (429, 502, 503, 504 and connection timeouts) are retried up to three times by re-enqueueing from the Finalizer with a MinimumQueueableDelayInMinutes backoff; 400, 401, 403, 404 and 422 write the failure record immediately with no retry.
decisions.branch_quote: ├── Known 429 throttling                    → Queueable with exponential backoff + Finalizer
decisions.rationale: Q7 supplies the classification table verbatim. skills/apex/apex-queueable-patterns bounds the pattern: the delay caps at 10 minutes and a Finalizer may re-enqueue a failed job five consecutive times, so three attempts sits inside both ceilings. HttpClient.retryOnTransient is deliberately off because its backoff is a busy-wait that burns Apex CPU.
alternatives_rejected: a hand-rolled retry loop inside execute()
decisions.consequences: A permanent failure surfaces in under a second rather than after three pointless retries, and a 401 never becomes a lockout - but anything needing more than three attempts or more than ten minutes of backoff is out of this pattern and lands in the failure record as Abandoned.

decisions.decision: Every webhook POST carries an Idempotency-Key header built from the Case Id and the escalation timestamp captured at enqueue time.
decisions.branch_quote: ├── Idempotency key required                → Generate in Apex, send as header; tie to Request_Id__c
decisions.rationale: Q8 confirms the tool accepts an Idempotency-Key header and names the Case Id plus the escalation timestamp as the key. The tree's 'tie to Request_Id__c' is adapted: this build has no Request_Id__c and the same string is stored on the failure record instead, so a resend replays the identical key.
alternatives_rejected: No key, accepting a possible double-page on an ambiguous 5xx
decisions.consequences: A retry after an ambiguous transport failure cannot page twice; the cost is that the key must be captured once at enqueue and carried through every retry rather than recomputed, which is what assumption A10 records.

decisions.decision: A Queueable Finalizer, attached as the first statement of execute(), is what guarantees the failure record is written - including when the job dies on a limit or unhandled exception.
decisions.branch_quote: ├── Yes → Use a Queueable Finalizer to dispatch the compensating action
decisions.rationale: Q15 requires the failure record on every terminal state. skills/apex/apex-queueable-patterns is explicit that try/catch cannot survive a limit exception that terminates the transaction and that the Finalizer runs either way, with FinalizerContext.getResult() returning SUCCESS or UNHANDLED_EXCEPTION.
alternatives_rejected: a platform event published from the catch block
decisions.consequences: The Finalizer runs in its own transaction under synchronous governor limits, so it must stay thin - it records and re-enqueues, and does not do the work over again.

decisions.decision: The escalation-detection automation is Apex - a Case after-update trigger delegating to a handler and a service layer - not a record-triggered Flow.
decisions.branch_quote: ├── Yes  → Apex (trigger + handler + service layer)
decisions.rationale: Q3's list is satisfied on two counts: callouts that need retry and backoff, and a deployable unit under an enforced coverage gate with assertion-style tests. The tree's own note that 'one straightforward callout is NOT on this list' does not apply - the classification table in Q7, the Finalizer, the idempotency key and the resend path are the opposite of straightforward. Q13 also places the enqueue in the after-update handler's service layer.
alternatives_rejected: After-save record-triggered Flow with an InvocableMethod callout action
Flow plus an Apex invocable per automation-selection Q6
decisions.consequences: Apex carries a 75% org-wide coverage gate Flow does not, and the fault path is a failure record this build owns rather than a Flow error email - which is also why Q40, Q41 and Q42 are out of scope.

decisions.decision: The ops dashboard is fed by a Tier2_Escalation__e platform event it consumes through the Pub/Sub API, not by a second direct callout or an internal service call.
decisions.branch_quote: ├── Yes → Platform Event + Pub/Sub API gRPC subscriber
decisions.rationale: The requirement states the dashboard is a separate system already subscribed to Salesforce platform events, and Q39 confirms no internal Apex or Flow subscriber exists. The tree's delivery-allocation note applies: an API subscriber draws on the 24-hour delivery allocation, and 15 escalations a day is far inside it.
alternatives_rejected: A second HTTP callout to the dashboard
decisions.consequences: Delivery is at-least-once and the dashboard dedupes its own duplicates (Q12); EventBus.publish returning success means queued, not delivered, which is why D10 requires the SaveResult to be inspected.

decisions.decision: Tier2_Escalation__e is declared with publishBehavior PublishAfterCommit and is published from the escalating transaction's service layer - before the Queueable runs - rather than from inside the Queueable's execute().
decisions.rationale: Q10 requires that a rolled-back escalation reach neither the on-call tool nor the dashboard, which PublishAfterCommit gives directly. The sequencing half is not in any tree: skills/apex/apex-queueable-patterns states that callouts are impossible after DML in the same transaction, and a publish-after-commit publish is a DML statement, so publishing inside execute() before the callout would break the callout. Publishing in the trigger transaction also means the dashboard sees the escalation regardless of webhook outcome, which was Q9's proposed sequencing default. Q11 requires the publish SaveResult to be checked and a failed publish logged to the same failure object.
alternatives_rejected: Publish inside the Queueable before the callout
publish inside the Queueable after the callout, carrying the callout outcome
decisions.consequences: The event carries no callout outcome - the dashboard learns that an escalation happened, not whether the page landed - and a failed publish is a separate Integration_Failure__c row from a failed webhook.

decisions.decision: The hourly channel-health check is Schedulable Apex whose execute() only enqueues a Queueable, not a schedule-triggered Flow.
decisions.branch_quote: ├── Clock (cron)                     → Schedulable wrapper that enqueues Queueable
decisions.rationale: Q24 delegates the choice to this tree, and standards/decision-trees/README.md assigns Schedulable-versus-Scheduled-Flow to async-selection.md rather than to automation-selection.md or flow-pattern-selector.md. The cadence is the reason it does not fall out to Flow: flow-pattern-selector.md Q6 gates a schedule-triggered flow on a daily, weekly or monthly cadence, and this is hourly. The library also disagrees with itself on whether a scheduled flow can run hourly at all - skills/flow/flow-time-based-patterns says it can, skills/flow/scheduled-flows says the granularity may not fit - which is a second reason not to build on it.
alternatives_rejected: a Flow scheduled path on Integration_Failure__c
decisions.consequences: Schedulable Apex runs under synchronous governor limits and cannot call out, which is fine for two aggregate queries and an email, and the CRON literal makes the hourly cadence explicit and deployable rather than a Setup-time choice.

decisions.decision: Integration_Failure__c ships with a Private org-wide default, and the three Support Engineering admins get every row through object-scoped View All Records / Modify All Records on the Tier2_Webhook_Admin permission set rather than through a sharing rule.
decisions.branch_quote: ├── Public Read-Only / Public Read-Write    → Tighten OWD before adding anything → Q2
decisions.rationale: Q19 and Q20 answer CRUD/FLS and the resend owner but not record visibility. The tree's Q1 rules out shipping a Public Read/Write default; its 'Permission sets vs sharing' table then places this case - 'Can user bypass sharing to do admin things?' - on View/Modify All at object scope, to be used for narrow admin permission sets, which Tier2_Webhook_Admin is. A criteria-based sharing rule was rejected because the criterion would be 'every row', which is a whole-object grant wearing a rule's clothes.
alternatives_rejected: View All Data on the permission set
decisions.consequences: The grant is object-scoped and auditable in one named set, and check_permission_set_architecture.py reports it as a sharing-bypass WARN by design rather than as an error; the trade is that anyone holding Tier2_Webhook_Admin sees every failure row including its stored request payload.

decisions.decision: Cross-transaction duplicate suppression uses the Case.Tier2_Notified_At__c stamp with a ten-minute window, not AsyncOptions.DuplicateSignature.
decisions.rationale: Q14 chose this mechanism explicitly. The skill's own canonical answer to the same question is DuplicateSignature, which suppresses across transactions where a static guard cannot; it is recorded as the rejected alternative rather than silently dropped. The field stamp was chosen because it is also the audit trail an admin reads on the Case, and because a suppressed DuplicateSignature enqueue throws DuplicateMessageException rather than no-op'ing, which would need its own catch.
alternatives_rejected: AsyncOptions.DuplicateSignature built from the Case Id
decisions.consequences: The window is wall-clock rather than transactional, so two escalations of the same Case eleven minutes apart both page - which is the intended behaviour - and a Case whose webhook never succeeded is never stamped, so it is never suppressed.

decisions.decision: Tier2_Webhook_Admin is assigned to every user who can escalate a Case to Tier 2 and to the user who schedules the hourly health check, because the Queueable calls out as the user whose save enqueued it and scheduled Apex runs as the user who scheduled the job - neither is the Automated Process entity.
decisions.rationale: Q23 asserts the Automated Process entity and asks the plan to settle how it gets the principal grant. The skill states that async Apex runs as the async context user - the user who fired the async, except for scheduled jobs and platform-event triggers - and skills/flow/flow-and-platform-events records that Automated Process holds no profile and no permission set assignments, so the grant Q19 describes cannot be made to it at all. skills/apex/apex-named-credentials-patterns is the matching rule from the credential side: the permission set must be assigned to the user the transaction runs as, which for Queueable Apex is not necessarily whoever started the work. The same rule settles M1-S04: skills/apex/apex-user-and-permission-checks names the scheduler as the running user for a scheduled job, so the scheduling user needs the same permission set for read on Integration_Failure__c and on Case.Tier2_Notified_At__c. That user is inside the assignee set only if they can also escalate a Case, which nothing guarantees, so the set is stated as the union of the two rather than left to coincidence.
alternatives_rejected: Assigning the permission set to the three admins only
granting the principal to the Automated Process entity
moving the callout into a platform-event-triggered subscriber so it does run as Automated Process
decisions.consequences: The assignee list is wider than Q19 anticipated - every user who can escalate, plus the scheduling user - and is an access decision a human signs at the M1-S02 gate. If it is wrong the failure is loud rather than silent: every escalation returns 401 and lands in the failure record, and the hourly check throws on the first query. Assumption A2 carries the library's own hedge on the word 'often' and A13 carries the scheduling-user half.

steps.title: Case escalation trigger, publish-and-enqueue service, webhook Queueable with Finalizer retry, resend path and tests

inputs.feature_summary: When a Case owner changes to the Tier_2_Engineering queue on after update, publish a Tier2_Escalation__e event for the ops dashboard and enqueue one Queueable for the whole transaction that POSTs each escalated Case to the on-call tool through the OnCall_Tool Named Credential, retrying transient failures from a Finalizer and leaving an Integration_Failure__c row for every failure. This is one feature, not two: the second trigger, on Integration_Failure__c, does nothing but re-enter the same Queueable when an admin ticks Resend, so it adds a call site rather than a second unit of work - it emits no callout, no event and no class the escalation path does not already need.
inputs.detection: After update on Case: OwnerId changed in this save to the Tier_2_Engineering queue (assumption A12). The queue developer name is resolved to a Group Id, never written as a literal: a private static Map<String, Id> populated once per transaction from SELECT Id, DeveloperName FROM Group WHERE Type = 'Queue', read through a queueId(String devName) accessor - the shape in skills/apex/apex-hardcoded-id-elimination/references/examples.md Example 3, 'Group/Queue assignment for Case routing'. One SOQL per transaction, no Id literal, and the same code deploys to every org. A hardcoded Group Id is not the fallback: apex-builder's REFUSAL_SECURITY_GUARD clause (d) refuses it. The queue is assumed to exist (assumption A8).
inputs.enqueue_contract: Exactly one Queueable per transaction carrying every escalated Case Id in that transaction, never one per Case (Q13). The enqueue ceiling is 50 per synchronous transaction and exactly one per asynchronous transaction, which is why a per-Case enqueue in the handler is wrong even though it passes a single-record test.
inputs.ordering_constraint: The platform event publish happens in the escalating transaction's service layer, before the Queueable runs; the callout happens first inside the Queueable's execute() and the DML that writes Integration_Failure__c and stamps Case.Tier2_Notified_At__c happens after it. A callout cannot follow DML in the same transaction, which is decision D10's second half.
inputs.publish_result: EventBus.publish never throws for a rejected event; the SaveResult is the only failure signal (Q11). A failed publish writes an Integration_Failure__c row with Severity__c Error, distinct from a failed webhook row.
inputs.retry_contract: Transient: 429, 502, 503, 504 and connection timeouts, retried up to three times; permanent: 400, 401, 403, 404, 422, no retry (Q7). Retry is a Finalizer re-enqueue with an AsyncOptions MinimumQueueableDelayInMinutes backoff; the delay caps at 10 minutes and a Finalizer may re-enqueue a failed job five consecutive times, so three attempts sits inside both ceilings. inputs.finalizer_contract: System.attachFinalizer is the first statement of execute(). inputs.feature_summary: An hourly scheduled job that counts Integration_Failure__c rows created in the last hour and Cases stamped with Tier2_Notified_At__c in the last day, and emails Support Engineering from the org-wide address when more than three failures landed in the hour or when no success has occurred in 24 hours while escalations exist.
inputs.thresholds: Alert when Integration_Failure__c rows created in the last hour exceed three, OR when no Case has been stamped with Tier2_Notified_At__c in the last 24 hours while at least one escalation occurred in that window (Q24).
inputs.cadence: Hourly. The CRON literal is six or seven whitespace-separated fields in the order Seconds Minutes Hours Day_of_month Month Day_of_week Optional_year, with '?' in one of the two day fields - the checker rejects anything else.
inputs.shape: Schedulable execute() only enqueues a Queueable and does nothing else: scheduled Apex runs under synchronous governor limits and cannot make callouts, and the async tree's own default is that a Schedulable body delegates immediately (decision D11).
inputs.sender: The org-wide email address support-noreply@acme.example, set on the outbound message. It has no metadata type and cannot be deployed by this build - assumption A4 records it as a deploy prerequisite that must already be verified in the target org.
inputs.recipients: Support Engineering (Q24). The distribution list address is taken from the deploy-order note rather than hardcoded per environment.
inputs.running_user: Scheduled Apex runs as the user who scheduled the job - not the escalating user and not Automated Process. That user needs read on Integration_Failure__c and on Case.Tier2_Notified_At__c, and in API 67.0 default user mode both queries enforce their FLS with no keyword at all. Tier2_Webhook_Admin from M1-S02 now carries both halves: the Integration_Failure__c object and field permissions and the Case.Tier2_Notified_At__c field permission (PV-001). The scheduling user is inside the decision D14 assignee set by that decision's own wording - it is the union of everyone who can escalate a Case and the user who schedules this job - and assumption A13 records that membership as something to confirm rather than assume.
inputs.scheduling: System.schedule is a post-deploy step recorded in the deploy-order note, not something this step performs. Aborting a prior job of the same name is required before rescheduling - a duplicate job name throws.
inputs.tests: System.schedule inside Test.startTest()/Test.stopTest(); assert the CronTrigger or AsyncApexJob row exists and that the alert branch fires on seeded data and stays silent below the thresholds.
inputs.unverified: None on the mechanism. The library disagrees with itself on whether a schedule-triggered Flow supports an hourly cadence - skills/flow/flow-time-based-patterns lists hourly as available, skills/flow/scheduled-flows says the granularity may not fit - and decision D11 routes away from Flow rather than resolving that disagreement.

plan.title: Tier 2 escalation webhook and platform event

requirement.summary: Build a Tier 2 Case-escalation notification path: when a Case moves into the existing Tier_2_Engineering queue, an Apex Queueable (enqueued off the escalation-triggering automation, authenticated via a Named Credential + External Credential holding the on-call tool's API key) posts case number, severity, subject and a case link to an HTTPS on-call-tool webhook with status-code-based retry, and the same escalation publishes a Platform Event that an already-subscribed internal ops dashboard consumes; every delivery attempt lands on a new, admin-visible failure/audit record with a manual resend action, and the API key is held only in an External Credential, never in code or a Custom Setting.

clarifications.question: Per standards/decision-trees/integration-pattern-selection.md Direction 1 (Salesforce calls out): confirm the on-call webhook call is fire-and-forget (Queueable, not Continuation, since no user watches a spinner), authenticated via Named Credential + External Credential (Custom header / API key per Q2), and retried per a status-code classification (Q4) — does the on-call tool's actual contract match this shape, or does it require something else (e.g. a synchronous ack, OAuth instead of a static key)?
clarifications.why: This is the tree's own top-level direction/auth/retry checklist; a wrong call here is a rebuild of the whole integration shape, not a tweak.
clarifications.proposed_default: Fire-and-forget Queueable, Named Credential + External Credential with Custom header (API key), retry classified by status code.
clarifications.answer_shape: A direction/auth/retry row naming the pattern actually used, or the deviation and why.
clarifications.answer: Confirmed: Direction 1 only — Salesforce calls out to the on-call tool's HTTPS REST endpoint (JSON POST). Nothing calls into Salesforce for this feature.

clarifications.question: Reject the legacy Outbound Message / Workflow Rule action mechanism in favor of a Named-Credential-based Apex callout for the on-call notification — confirm?
clarifications.why: Outbound Message's host (Workflow Rules) reached end of support 31 Dec 2025, cannot express JSON + API-key auth cleanly (it expects a SOAP Ack envelope), and this decision determines every downstream metadata choice.
clarifications.proposed_default: Yes — use a Named-Credential-based Apex callout, not Outbound Message.
clarifications.answer_shape: A yes/no plus the rejected-alternative reason recorded in decisions.md.
clarifications.answer: Yes. Reject Outbound Message / Workflow Rule. Use a Named Credential + Apex callout so the key lives in an External Credential and retries/failure records are under our control.

clarifications.question: Is the on-call tool's Named Credential built on the Legacy model or the enhanced SecuredEndpoint model (separate External Credential)?
clarifications.why: Every field the Legacy shape relies on is deprecated at API 56.0; building new metadata on it means building on a deprecated surface.
clarifications.proposed_default: SecuredEndpoint (Named Credential + separate External Credential).
clarifications.answer_shape: The namedCredentialType value and the file count it implies (2 vs 1).
clarifications.answer: Enhanced model: a Named Credential on top of a separate External Credential (SecuredEndpoint). No legacy Named Credential.

clarifications.question: Named principal or per-user principal for the on-call tool's External Credential?
clarifications.why: Only Named Principal works from Batch, Queueable and Scheduled Apex — this design requires a Queueable, so the principal type is not a free choice.
clarifications.proposed_default: Named Principal — required for the Queueable-based callout.
clarifications.answer_shape: NamedPrincipal vs PerUserPrincipal, with the Queueable constraint cited as the reason.
clarifications.answer: Named principal — one service API key for the whole org. Per-user principals are not wanted; the on-call tool has one integration user.

clarifications.question: Who owns the Authorization header on the webhook call — does the External Credential inject it (generateAuthorizationHeader default true), or does the Apex code build it explicitly?
clarifications.why: Apex adding its own header on top of the platform default is a documented collision that surfaces as a 401.
clarifications.proposed_default: The platform / External Credential owns it; Apex does not set an Authorization header itself.
clarifications.answer_shape: One named owner for the header, encoded in the External Credential metadata.
clarifications.answer: The External Credential injects the API key as a custom header; Apex never reads or builds the Authorization/API-key header and never sees the secret.

clarifications.question: Does the on-call tool expect the API key in a specific custom header name, or in the request body?
clarifications.why: This decides the External Credential parameter shape ({!$Credential.*} merge field target) and whether allowMergeFieldsInHeader / allowMergeFieldsInBody must be enabled — both default false.
clarifications.answer_shape: The exact header name (or body path) the vendor's API documents.
clarifications.answer: A custom header named X-API-Key (the tool's documented header). The request body is JSON.

clarifications.question: For the on-call tool's API specifically, which HTTP status codes are transient/retryable (e.g. 429, 503) and which indicate a hard failure that should go straight to the visible failure record (e.g. 401, 422)?
clarifications.why: Retryable vs non-retryable cannot be inferred from the status code alone; retrying a 401 is a lockout, not a fix.
clarifications.answer_shape: A status-code classification table the retry logic and its tests both read.
clarifications.answer: Transient/retryable: 429, 502, 503, 504 and connection timeouts (retry up to 3 times with backoff). Permanent: 400, 401, 403, 404, 422 — no retry, write the failure record immediately.

clarifications.question: Is the webhook POST safe to send twice, and does the on-call tool accept/require an idempotency key?
clarifications.why: A 5xx or transport failure means unknown, not failed; retrying without a key can double-page the same escalation.
clarifications.answer_shape: Either a documented idempotency-key header, or an explicit no-retry-on-ambiguous-outcome decision.
clarifications.answer: Yes, the POST is safe to send twice; the tool accepts an Idempotency-Key header. Use the Case Id plus the escalation timestamp as the key.

clarifications.question: Per standards/decision-trees/async-selection.md Q2-Q4: confirm the escalation-triggered work is fire-and-forget (not user-facing), runs from a Queueable (AllowsCallouts) enqueued off the Case-escalation automation, and decide the publish sequencing — does the platform event publish before the callout (dashboard sees the escalation immediately regardless of webhook outcome) or after it (event carries the callout's outcome too)?
clarifications.why: This is the tree's own entry-point classification plus the one sequencing decision the tree does not make for you; it changes what the Queueable's execute() actually does and in what order.
clarifications.proposed_default: Publish the platform event first (dashboard visibility should not depend on webhook success), then attempt the callout with retry.
clarifications.answer_shape: The chosen sequencing, with the rejected order's reason recorded.
clarifications.answer: Fire-and-forget: no user waits on the result. It must complete within a minute of the escalation, which a Queueable enqueued from the after-update handler satisfies.

clarifications.question: If the Case-escalation transaction that triggers this automation rolls back, must the on-call tool and the ops dashboard still be notified?
clarifications.why: Decides the Platform Event object's publishBehavior element; omitting it defaults to PublishImmediately, which fires regardless of rollback.
clarifications.proposed_default: No — publish only after the Case save commits (PublishAfterCommit); a rolled-back escalation should not page anyone.
clarifications.answer_shape: The explicit publishBehavior value and which limit meter the publisher spends.
clarifications.answer: If the escalation transaction rolls back, nothing must reach the on-call tool or the dashboard. Enqueue the callout and publish the event only when the transaction commits (publish-after-commit semantics).

clarifications.question: What is the worst-case impact if one escalation's platform event is silently lost (EventBus.publish success only means 'queued', not 'delivered')?
clarifications.why: Decides whether checking Database.SaveResult is enough or an EventPublishFailureCallback plus a logged-failure path is required.
clarifications.answer_shape: Either an accepted-risk note, or the failure callback wired into the same failure record as the webhook path.
clarifications.answer: Worst case a Severity 1 escalation is missing from the ops dashboard. The webhook is the primary channel; a lost event is tolerable when the webhook succeeded, but the publish result must be checked and a failed publish logged in the same failure record object.

clarifications.question: What happens if the ops dashboard processes the same escalation event twice (Platform Events deliver at-least-once)?
clarifications.why: Decides whether the event payload needs a stable EventUuid / case number the dashboard can dedupe on, which is a contract with a team this build does not own.
clarifications.proposed_default: Dashboard dedupes on case number / EventUuid; document as a contract with the dashboard's owning team, not solved on the Salesforce side.
clarifications.answer_shape: The dedupe key named in the event schema, and confirmation the dashboard team has agreed to use it.
clarifications.answer: The dashboard team will dedupe on case number + escalation time; duplicate events are acceptable. Do not add Salesforce-side dedupe for the event.

clarifications.question: Where is the callout Queueable enqueued from (the escalation-triggering automation directly, or a service layer), and could that same code path ever run from inside another async job?
clarifications.why: The enqueue ceiling differs by context — 50 per synchronous transaction, exactly 1 per asynchronous transaction — and a callout cannot follow DML in the same execute().
clarifications.answer_shape: The one call site that owns the enqueue, and confirmation it is never itself inside another async transaction.
clarifications.answer: Enqueued from the Case after-update trigger handler's service layer: one Queueable per transaction carrying every escalated Case Id in that transaction (bulk-safe), not one per case.

clarifications.question: Can the same escalation be enqueued twice from two different transactions (e.g. a re-save, a duplicate escalation trigger firing)? If so, is cross-transaction dedup needed?
clarifications.why: A static in-memory guard resets at the transaction boundary; only AsyncOptions.DuplicateSignature suppresses duplicates across transactions, and a suppressed enqueue throws rather than silently no-op'ing.
clarifications.answer_shape: The stable business key (likely Case Id) the DuplicateSignature is built from, and the catch that turns the exception into a no-op.
clarifications.answer: Yes, a re-save can re-fire. Stamp a new field Case.Tier2_Notified_At__c when the webhook succeeds and skip cases already stamped within the last 10 minutes.

clarifications.question: When the Queueable throws an unhandled or limit exception, must the failure record still get written?
clarifications.why: try/catch cannot survive a limit exception that terminates the transaction; only a Finalizer runs either way, and its budget is five consecutive re-enqueues.
clarifications.proposed_default: Yes — a Finalizer writes/updates the failure record on both SUCCESS and UNHANDLED_EXCEPTION, since that is the only guaranteed hook.
clarifications.answer_shape: The Finalizer's behavior on each terminal state, named explicitly.
clarifications.answer: Yes. The failure record must be written even when the Queueable dies on an unhandled or limit exception — use a Queueable Finalizer for that.

clarifications.question: Where does the visible failure record live — a new custom object dedicated to this integration, or does Apex already have a sink (e.g. templates/apex/custom_objects/Application_Log__c) that should be reused/extended instead of inventing a new one?
clarifications.why: One sink is queryable, correlatable and reportable; two sinks are two half-monitored portfolios that need a join nobody has written.
clarifications.answer_shape: One named object (new or reused), and a reason if a new one is chosen over the existing log sink.
clarifications.answer: A new custom object dedicated to this integration: Integration_Failure__c. We have no existing Apex log object in the org.

clarifications.question: What does the status/severity picklist on the failure record contain, and does the Apex code send exactly those values?
clarifications.why: A required + restricted picklist that the sending code doesn't match exactly makes the fault-path write itself fault, and then nothing is logged at all.
clarifications.proposed_default: A restricted picklist (e.g. Pending / Failed / Retrying / Resolved) with values matching the Apex enum exactly.
clarifications.answer_shape: The exact picklist value list, cross-checked against the Apex constant list.
clarifications.answer: Status picklist: New, Retrying, Resent, Resolved, Abandoned. Severity picklist: Error, Warning. Apex must write exactly those values and nothing else.

clarifications.question: What fields must the failure record carry to make a resend actionable?

clarifications.proposed_default: Case lookup, Request_Payload__c (long text), Last_Error__c, Retry_Count__c, Status__c, Last_Attempted_Date__c.
clarifications.answer_shape: The field list, each with the value it must hold to support a one-click resend.
clarifications.answer: Case lookup, case number, endpoint, HTTP status, response body (first 32k chars), attempt count, last attempt time, error message, the JSON payload sent, Status, and a Resend checkbox the admin ticks.

POST one JSON notification per escalated Case to the on-call tool's HTTPS REST endpoint, carrying case number, severity, subject and a link back to the Case (requirement para 1; Q1, Q30, Q31).

Authenticate that call through a SecuredEndpoint Named Credential over a separate External Credential with a named principal, so the API key never appears in code or a custom setting (requirement para 4; Q2, Q3, Q4, Q5, Q6, Q25).
Classify the response: retry 429/502/503/504 and connection timeouts up to three times with backoff; write the failure record immediately on 400/401/403/404/422 (requirement para 2; Q7, Q15).
Send an Idempotency-Key header built from the Case Id and the escalation timestamp so a retry cannot double-page (Q8).

Publish a Tier2_Escalation__e platform event with PublishAfterCommit for the external ops dashboard, and check the publish result rather than assuming delivery (requirement para 2; Q10, Q11, Q12, Q39).
Create Integration_Failure__c with the diagnostic field set Q18 names, the restricted Status and Severity picklists Q17 fixes, and a Resend checkbox (requirement para 3; Q16, Q17, Q18).
Stamp Case.Tier2_Notified_At__c when the webhook succeeds, and skip a Case already stamped inside the last ten minutes, so a re-save does not re-page (Q14).
Grant the External Credential principal and Integration_Failure__c CRUD/FLS through a Tier2_Webhook_Admin permission set (Q19, Q20, Q23).
Re-send a failed notification when a Support Engineering admin ticks Resend on the failure record (requirement para 3; Q20).
Run an hourly channel-health check that emails Support Engineering when more than three failures land in an hour, or when no success has occurred in 24 hours while escalations exist (Q24).

Ship every artefact in one build-level package.xml with a written deploy order, including the Apex members the apex-builder steps cannot manifest themselves (Q25; standards/build-orchestration.md section 5, The Apex exception).
out: Any customer-facing change. The requirement states 'No customer-facing change' and Q44 confirms the audience is internal employees only, with no Experience Cloud or partner licence implication; nothing in this plan touches a site, a customer-visible layout or an external email.

The ops dashboard's Pub/Sub API subscriber, its authenticating principal, its IP allowlisting, its login-hour policy and its service-account ownership. Q32, Q33, Q34, Q35 and Q37 each record the subscription as already established and owned by the dashboard's own team.
Salesforce-side deduplication of the escalation event. Q12: the dashboard team dedupes on case number plus escalation time and accepts duplicate events, so no dedupe is built here.

Outbound Message / Workflow Rule mechanics - WSDL version, sending user, includeSessionId and the dead letter queue permission. Q26, Q27, Q28 and Q29 are all moot once Q2 rejected Outbound Message in favour of a Named-Credential Apex callout.
An in-Salesforce report or dashboard on notification failure rates. Q45: none requested beyond the external ops dashboard the platform event feeds.

Creating or changing the Tier_2_Engineering queue and the escalation rule that fills it. The requirement's closing paragraph states the existing case-intake build already provides them and this build may assume the queue exists (see assumption A8).

Verifying the org-wide email address support-noreply@acme.example. Q24 records it as a deploy prerequisite, and skills/admin/email-templates-and-alerts states that org-wide email addresses have no metadata type, so nothing in this build can deploy or verify it (see assumption A4).
Flow-based alternatives for the triggering automation and their fault routing. Q40, Q41 and Q42 are each conditional on choosing Flow, and decision D8 chose Apex.

Apex managed sharing, sharing rules or a criteria-based rule on Integration_Failure__c. Decision D12 settles record visibility with a Private OWD plus an object-scoped grant on one narrow admin permission set instead.

decisions.decision: Salesforce calls out to the on-call tool fire-and-forget from a Queueable implementing Database.AllowsCallouts; nothing calls into Salesforce for this feature.
decisions.branch_quote: No, fire-and-forget                    -> Queueable with AllowsCallouts
decisions.rationale: Q1's answer confirms Direction 1 only and Q9 confirms no user waits on the result, which is exactly this branch. Continuation is excluded because nobody watches a spinner; Batch is excluded because the volume is 15 a day peaking at 50 in five minutes (Q22).
alternatives_rejected: Outbound Message on a Workflow Rule
decisions.consequences: The notification is decoupled from the save, so a webhook outage never blocks a Support agent's escalation - and the only evidence a notification failed is the Integration_Failure__c row this build creates.

decisions.decision: Authenticate with a Named Credential over a separate External Credential using the Custom authentication protocol, with the API key injected as the X-API-Key header by the credential rather than by Apex.
decisions.branch_quote: Custom header / API key                 -> Named Credential + External Credential (Custom)
decisions.rationale: Q6 names X-API-Key as the tool's documented header and Q5 assigns header ownership to the platform, so generateAuthorizationHeader is deployed false and the header is an ExternalCredential AuthHeader parameter. Apex sets no credential header at all, so allowMergeFieldsInHeader stays false.
alternatives_rejected: API key in a Custom Setting or Custom Label
Apex-built Authorization header with an Apex-side {!$Credential.*} merge field
decisions.consequences: The secret is entered in Setup against the principal after deploy and is never in source, an export, or a sandbox refresh - which also means the deploy alone does not make the integration work: a human must enter the value and assign the permission set.

decisions.decision: The External Credential declares a NamedPrincipal, not a PerUserPrincipal, and the Named Credential is the enhanced SecuredEndpoint type rather than Legacy.
decisions.rationale: integration-pattern-selection.md Q2 routes to 'Named Credential + External Credential (Custom)' but does not choose between principal types or between the legacy and enhanced models; the skill's Decision Guidance does, on both counts - 'Async job (Batch / Queueable / Scheduled) -> NamedPrincipal' and 'every legacy field is deprecated at 56.0 - new work goes on SecuredEndpoint'. Q3 and Q4 answer the same way.
alternatives_rejected: Legacy Named Credential with an embedded endpoint and protocol
decisions.consequences: One shared service identity means the on-call tool's audit trail attributes every incident to Salesforce rather than to the escalating agent; the trade is that a per-user principal would not work from a Queueable at all.

decisions.decision: The webhook body is JSON, serialised and deserialised in Apex through templates/apex/HttpClient.cls rather than a hand-built HttpRequest.
decisions.branch_quote: JSON REST                               -> HttpClient + JSON.serialize/deserialize
decisions.rationale: Q1 and Q6 both describe a JSON POST. Q31 sizes the payload well under the 6MB/12MB ceilings, so no paging or chunking is needed.
alternatives_rejected: Raw HttpRequest construction in the Queueable
decisions.consequences: The endpoint, the timeout and the retry switch are all set through one builder the checker recognises, which is also why the per-Case callout loop does not trip check_callouts_and_http_integrations.py rule 4.

decisions.decision: Transient failures (429, 502, 503, 504 and connection timeouts) are retried up to three times by re-enqueueing from the Finalizer with a MinimumQueueableDelayInMinutes backoff; 400, 401, 403, 404 and 422 write the failure record immediately with no retry.
decisions.branch_quote: Known 429 throttling                    -> Queueable with exponential backoff + Finalizer
decisions.rationale: Q7 supplies the classification table verbatim. skills/apex/apex-queueable-patterns bounds the pattern: the delay caps at 10 minutes and a Finalizer may re-enqueue a failed job five consecutive times, so three attempts sits inside both ceilings. HttpClient.retryOnTransient is deliberately off because its backoff is a busy-wait that burns Apex CPU.
alternatives_rejected: a hand-rolled retry loop inside execute()
decisions.consequences: A permanent failure surfaces in under a second rather than after three pointless retries, and a 401 never becomes a lockout - but anything needing more than three attempts or more than ten minutes of backoff is out of this pattern and lands in the failure record as Abandoned.

decisions.decision: Every webhook POST carries an Idempotency-Key header built from the Case Id and the escalation timestamp captured at enqueue time.
decisions.branch_quote: Idempotency key required                -> Generate in Apex, send as header; tie to Request_Id__c
decisions.rationale: Q8 confirms the tool accepts an Idempotency-Key header and names the Case Id plus the escalation timestamp as the key. The tree's 'tie to Request_Id__c' is adapted: this build has no Request_Id__c and the same string is stored on the failure record instead, so a resend replays the identical key.
alternatives_rejected: No key, accepting a possible double-page on an ambiguous 5xx
decisions.consequences: A retry after an ambiguous transport failure cannot page twice; the cost is that the key must be captured once at enqueue and carried through every retry rather than recomputed, which is what assumption A10 records.

decisions.decision: A Queueable Finalizer, attached as the first statement of execute(), is what guarantees the failure record is written - including when the job dies on a limit or unhandled exception.
decisions.branch_quote: Yes -> Use a Queueable Finalizer to dispatch the compensating action
decisions.rationale: Q15 requires the failure record on every terminal state. skills/apex/apex-queueable-patterns is explicit that try/catch cannot survive a limit exception that terminates the transaction and that the Finalizer runs either way, with FinalizerContext.getResult() returning SUCCESS or UNHANDLED_EXCEPTION.
alternatives_rejected: a platform event published from the catch block
decisions.consequences: The Finalizer runs in its own transaction under synchronous governor limits, so it must stay thin - it records and re-enqueues, and does not do the work over again.

decisions.decision: The escalation-detection automation is Apex - a Case after-update trigger delegating to a handler and a service layer - not a record-triggered Flow.
decisions.branch_quote: Yes  -> Apex (trigger + handler + service layer)
decisions.rationale: Q3's list is satisfied on two counts: callouts that need retry and backoff, and a deployable unit under an enforced coverage gate with assertion-style tests. The tree's own note that 'one straightforward callout is NOT on this list' does not apply - the classification table in Q7, the Finalizer, the idempotency key and the resend path are the opposite of straightforward. Q13 also places the enqueue in the after-update handler's service layer.
alternatives_rejected: After-save record-triggered Flow with an InvocableMethod callout action
Flow plus an Apex invocable per automation-selection Q6
decisions.consequences: Apex carries a 75% org-wide coverage gate Flow does not, and the fault path is a failure record this build owns rather than a Flow error email - which is also why Q40, Q41 and Q42 are out of scope.

decisions.decision: The ops dashboard is fed by a Tier2_Escalation__e platform event it consumes through the Pub/Sub API, not by a second direct callout or an internal service call.
decisions.branch_quote: Yes -> Platform Event + Pub/Sub API gRPC subscriber
decisions.rationale: The requirement states the dashboard is a separate system already subscribed to Salesforce platform events, and Q39 confirms no internal Apex or Flow subscriber exists. The tree's delivery-allocation note applies: an API subscriber draws on the 24-hour delivery allocation, and 15 escalations a day is far inside it.
alternatives_rejected: A second HTTP callout to the dashboard
decisions.consequences: Delivery is at-least-once and the dashboard dedupes its own duplicates (Q12); EventBus.publish returning success means queued, not delivered, which is why D10 requires the SaveResult to be inspected.

decisions.decision: Tier2_Escalation__e is declared with publishBehavior PublishAfterCommit and is published from the escalating transaction's service layer - before the Queueable runs - rather than from inside the Queueable's execute().
decisions.rationale: Q10 requires that a rolled-back escalation reach neither the on-call tool nor the dashboard, which PublishAfterCommit gives directly. The sequencing half is not in any tree: skills/apex/apex-queueable-patterns states that callouts are impossible after DML in the same transaction, and a publish-after-commit publish is a DML statement, so publishing inside execute() before the callout would break the callout. Publishing in the trigger transaction also means the dashboard sees the escalation regardless of webhook outcome, which was Q9's proposed sequencing default. Q11 requires the publish SaveResult to be checked and a failed publish logged to the same failure object.
alternatives_rejected: Publish inside the Queueable before the callout
publish inside the Queueable after the callout, carrying the callout outcome
decisions.consequences: The event carries no callout outcome - the dashboard learns that an escalation happened, not whether the page landed - and a failed publish is a separate Integration_Failure__c row from a failed webhook.

decisions.decision: The hourly channel-health check is Schedulable Apex whose execute() only enqueues a Queueable, not a schedule-triggered Flow.
decisions.branch_quote: Clock (cron)                     -> Schedulable wrapper that enqueues Queueable
decisions.rationale: Q24 delegates the choice to this tree, and standards/decision-trees/README.md assigns Schedulable-versus-Scheduled-Flow to async-selection.md rather than to automation-selection.md or flow-pattern-selector.md. The cadence is the reason it does not fall out to Flow: flow-pattern-selector.md Q6 gates a schedule-triggered flow on a daily, weekly or monthly cadence, and this is hourly. The library also disagrees with itself on whether a scheduled flow can run hourly at all - skills/flow/flow-time-based-patterns says it can, skills/flow/scheduled-flows says the granularity may not fit - which is a second reason not to build on it.
alternatives_rejected: a Flow scheduled path on Integration_Failure__c
decisions.consequences: Schedulable Apex runs under synchronous governor limits and cannot call out, which is fine for two aggregate queries and an email, and the CRON literal makes the hourly cadence explicit and deployable rather than a Setup-time choice.

decisions.decision: Integration_Failure__c ships with a Private org-wide default, and the three Support Engineering admins get every row through object-scoped View All Records / Modify All Records on the Tier2_Webhook_Admin permission set rather than through a sharing rule.
decisions.branch_quote: Public Read-Only / Public Read-Write    -> Tighten OWD before adding anything -> Q2
decisions.rationale: Q19 and Q20 answer CRUD/FLS and the resend owner but not record visibility. The tree's Q1 rules out shipping a Public Read/Write default; its 'Permission sets vs sharing' table then places this case - 'Can user bypass sharing to do admin things?' - on View/Modify All at object scope, to be used for narrow admin permission sets, which Tier2_Webhook_Admin is. A criteria-based sharing rule was rejected because the criterion would be 'every row', which is a whole-object grant wearing a rule's clothes.
alternatives_rejected: View All Data on the permission set
decisions.consequences: The grant is object-scoped and auditable in one named set, and check_permission_set_architecture.py reports it as a sharing-bypass WARN by design rather than as an error; the trade is that anyone holding Tier2_Webhook_Admin sees every failure row including its stored request payload.

decisions.decision: Cross-transaction duplicate suppression uses the Case.Tier2_Notified_At__c stamp with a ten-minute window, not AsyncOptions.DuplicateSignature.
decisions.rationale: Q14 chose this mechanism explicitly. The skill's own canonical answer to the same question is DuplicateSignature, which suppresses across transactions where a static guard cannot; it is recorded as the rejected alternative rather than silently dropped. The field stamp was chosen because it is also the audit trail an admin reads on the Case, and because a suppressed DuplicateSignature enqueue throws DuplicateMessageException rather than no-op'ing, which would need its own catch.
alternatives_rejected: AsyncOptions.DuplicateSignature built from the Case Id
decisions.consequences: The window is wall-clock rather than transactional, so two escalations of the same Case eleven minutes apart both page - which is the intended behaviour - and a Case whose webhook never succeeded is never stamped, so it is never suppressed.

decisions.decision: Tier2_Webhook_Admin is assigned to every user who can escalate a Case to Tier 2, not only to the three Support Engineering admins, because the Queueable makes its callout as the user whose save enqueued it.
decisions.rationale: Q23 asserts the Automated Process entity and asks the plan to settle how it gets the principal grant. The skill states that async Apex runs as the async context user - the user who fired the async, except for scheduled jobs and platform-event triggers - and skills/flow/flow-and-platform-events records that Automated Process holds no profile and no permission set assignments, so the grant Q19 describes cannot be made to it at all. skills/apex/apex-named-credentials-patterns is the matching rule from the credential side: the permission set must be assigned to the user the transaction runs as, which for Queueable Apex is not necessarily whoever started the work.
alternatives_rejected: Assigning the permission set to the three admins only
granting the principal to the Automated Process entity
moving the callout into a platform-event-triggered subscriber so it does run as Automated Process
decisions.consequences: The assignee list is wider than Q19 anticipated and is an access decision a human signs at the M1-S02 gate. If it is wrong, every escalation returns 401 and every escalation lands in the failure record - a loud failure rather than a silent one. Assumption A2 carries the library's own hedge on the word 'often'.

fields_on_integration_failure: Case__c - Lookup(Case), the escalated Case (Q18)
Case_Number__c - Text(30), denormalised so the row stays readable after a Case delete (Q18)
Endpoint__c - Text(255), the callout: path actually used (Q18)
HTTP_Status__c - Number(3,0), the status code returned (Q18)
Response_Body__c - LongTextArea(32768), first 32k characters of the response (Q18)
Attempt_Count__c - Number(2,0), how many attempts this row represents (Q18)
Last_Attempted_At__c - DateTime, the last attempt time (Q18)
Error_Message__c - LongTextArea(4000), the exception or classification message (Q18)
